description: We are a teenage teams and that's it
summary: Lunar Site Navigator is a web tool that helps choose where and when to land near the lunar south pole. A user picks any point on the Moon (or one of 18 real and planned landing sites) and a date. The tool reconstructs the real local horizon from NASA LRO LOLA terrain and shows when the Sun and Earth are above it: power windows, direct-to-Earth line-of-sight windows, time to sunset, eclipses, slope and crater hazards. It then gives a clear preliminary verdict: suitable, caution or not suitable. This matters because near the pole a few hundred metres or a few days can decide whether a lander has power and contact with Earth. Sun and Earth positions agree with NASA JPL Horizons to within 0.004°, and the tool reproduces the sunset that ended Firefly's Blue Ghost mission (16 March 2025).
details:
What it does

Near the lunar south pole the Sun stays within a few degrees of the horizon, and mountains often block both sunlight and the view of Earth. A few hundred metres or a few days can change everything. Our tool answers four questions for any site and date: Is there sunlight? Is Earth in view? How long until sunset? Is the ground safe?

How to use it

- Pick a site on the 3D Moon or from the list, and set the landing date.

- The panel shows the verdict, the checks behind it and the time to sunset.

- Tabs: Sky (real horizon with the Sun and Earth), 30 days and Windows (power and line-of-sight windows), Nearby (better spots within a few km), Dates (launch delays and best dates), Year, and Compare (up to 3 sites).

- 3D view: a descent with steep areas highlighted, and a month of sunlight in 15 seconds.

- Replay a real mission, export a mission briefing (PNG) or hourly data (CSV).

- Simple mode for everyone, Expert mode for engineers (thresholds, mast height, energy calculator). English and Russian.

How it works

For each site we trace a 360° horizon through NASA LOLA terrain, including lunar curvature: 80 m near the pole, 240 m at 80–87°S, about 3.8 km elsewhere. Sun and Earth positions come from astronomy-engine with the IAU lunar rotation model. Crater and cliff hazards come from the LOLA 5 m product. The verdict is the worst of six checks: slope, hazards, light at landing, time to sunset, sunlight and Earth visibility during the mission.

Validation

- Compared with NASA JPL Horizons for 8 sites over 30 days: maximum difference 0.0038°.

- Blue Ghost Mission 1: the predicted sunset date (16 March 2025) matches the end of the mission.

- The 14 March 2025 eclipse seen from the Moon is reproduced in time.

Impact

Mission planners can screen sites and dates in seconds, and students and the public can understand why landing at the south pole is hard.

Tools

HTML, CSS, JavaScript, three.js and astronomy-engine in the browser; Python (NumPy, Matplotlib) on Google Colab to prepare NASA data; Netlify for hosting; CapCut for the demo video.

AI assistance: AI chat assistants were used for brainstorming, research, coding and debugging. All results were checked by the team against NASA JPL Horizons. The demo voice-over is AI text-to-speech.

Limitations

This is a preliminary assessment from orbital data, not a landing certification. Boulders smaller than about 5 m are not resolved, and Earth visibility is geometric line of sight, not a guaranteed radio link.
